title: Written Analysis Rubric (Clinical Informatics)
description: For module capstones and the final implementation proposal. The point is defensibility under examiner-style scrutiny, not polish.

levels.descriptor: Factual errors about standards, workflows, regulations, or clinical reasoning that would fail a board question.
Mostly accurate but with imprecisions a careful examiner would catch (e.g., conflating SNOMED with LOINC).
Accurate. Standards, regulations, and clinical claims would survive a fellowship-level read.
Accurate AND the writer flags the contested or evolving parts of the field rather than presenting them as settled.
Assertions without support. Recommendations do not follow from the analysis.
Some reasoning, but key steps are skipped or rest on undefended assumptions.
The argument follows. A skeptical reader can trace each step from problem to recommendation.
The argument follows AND the writer flags its weakest link before a critic has to.
No counter-argument considered. Or only a strawman version.
A counter-argument appears but is dismissed without being taken seriously.
A real counter-argument — the one a skeptical CMIO would actually raise — is engaged and answered.
The strongest version is steel-manned, and the response either holds or the writer updates the recommendation.
Avoids the field's frameworks (CDS Five Rights, Sittig-Singh, SAFER, etc.) or uses them as labels.
Frameworks named but not load-bearing in the analysis.
Frameworks are doing real work — the analysis would be visibly weaker without them.
Frameworks are doing real work AND the writer notes where the framework itself fits the case poorly.
Generic, hedged, or AI-flavored prose. Reader cannot tell who wrote it or what they think.
Some personal stake visible but mostly safe and recycled.
Clear voice. The writer is in the room.
Clear voice AND visible intellectual honesty about uncertainty or change of mind.
